results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book (*Digital Compositing for Film and Video*) says you can build a basic chroma keyer yourself, but it's mostly a learning exercise — off-the-shelf keyers are hard to beat.

**What it is.** A chroma keyer takes an RGB image and converts it internally to HSV (or HSL), because it needs to distinguish saturation, which isn't an RGB attribute, alongside hue and luminance. It sets a starting pixel value as the "center" of the key, then defines separate ranges for Hue, Saturation, and Value: pixels inside those ranges go to 100% white, pixels outside go to black, and adjustable tolerances soften the matte edges [S13]. Because it keys on both color and brightness, it is far more discriminating than a luma key [S14].

**How to make one.** The recipe parallels the homemade luma keyer (Section 2.1.3):

1. Add an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV.
2. Pipe the HSV image into a color curve node.
3. Remember the channel remapping: the **RED curve now holds Hue**, the **GREEN curve holds Saturation**, and the **BLUE curve holds Value (brightness)**.
4. Adjust the three curves to include or exclude the Hue, Saturation, and Value ranges of the target object [S1].

The only materials you need are software with an HSV conversion plus color curves, and a test image: the book points you to its *Chroma key target.tif*, a colorful picture meant for practicing chroma and luma keys [S5]. A fancier variation, the "3D chroma keyer," works on different principles — it plots backing-color pixels inside the RGB color cube and keys on any arbitrary color, using a grossly simplified version of Primatte's approach [S7].

**The practical caveat.** The book is frank: unlike the homemade luma keyer, where cleverness can genuinely improve on the basic tool, rolling your own chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than it's worth" — try it once to test your mettle, but don't expect to beat a commercial keyer [S2]. Its general workflow advice is to try a chroma key first because it's quick, and only if the edges aren't good enough, switch to a color difference key like Keylight or Ultimatte, which usually produces nicer edges [S15]. One terminology warning accompanies all this: strictly speaking, a "chroma keyer" converts to HSV/HSL and keys on chrominance and luminance, so most greenscreen keyers are actually color difference keyers, not chroma keyers — Primatte being the notable exception [S4].

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
The book’s core point is that a **nonsquare pixel** is simply one whose width is not the same as its height, and the ratio of that width to height is the **pixel aspect ratio** [S3][S4]. On a properly adjusted computer monitor, pixels are square — a 1:1 pixel aspect ratio — but film and video formats often display an image whose shape differs from the underlying digital data, which is what makes the pixels "nonsquare" [S1][S2].

Crucially, the book insists this is a display convention, not a property of the image data. A system that can "display nonsquare pixels" applies a temporary geometric transform — an *unsqueeze* — so the image appears as it will in its final form; if you looked at the monitor with a magnifying glass, every pixel would still look properly proportioned, and the underlying image data is never modified [S5].

Two things about nonsquare pixels can trip up a compositor:

- **Pixel aspect ratio is not image aspect ratio.** The two are usually different numbers. In NTSC analog video, for example, the pixel aspect ratio is 10:11, meaning pixels are slightly taller than wide; a digitally created perfect circle sent straight to NTSC would appear as an ellipse stretched 11/10ths vertically unless you compensate (manually or via an automated system) [S13].
- **Rotation distorts squeezed images.** The most dramatic case is the anamorphic Cinemascope format, whose 2:1 squeeze the book uses for illustration — everything said about it applies equally to squeezed film or video [S6][S8]. If you rotate an element while it is still squeezed, the result stays distorted; the correct order is to unsqueeze, rotate, then resqueeze along the x-axis [S10]. Even a subtle 5° rotation leaves a visible error on a round subject, so the book's practical advice is to double-check everything when working with nonsquare pixels [S10].

In cinema context, this terminology also overlaps with *squeezed* and *anamorphic* formats — film whose image has been optically distorted and can be restored to its original shape [S8]. Relatedly, standard-definition video (720 × 480 NTSC, 720 × 576 PAL) uses rectangular nonsquare pixels, while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors all use square pixels [S9].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The *Miscellaneous Drawing Tips* pages in Francis Glebas' *Directing the Story* are a practical grab-bag of storyboard-drawing rules, and nearly every one circles back to the same goal: serve the story with drawings that are clear, expressive, and easy to read. The tips group into roughly five concerns.

**Clarity and intent.** Draw for clarity, with one idea per sketch, and have something to say in the image rather than just doodling [S2]. Highlight the one important idea of the sketch and subordinate everything else to it, and don't get clever with tricky camera angles, which often just make the drawing ambiguous [S5]. The book's related "Show and Tell" note makes the same point: draw attention to one idea at a time, just as you would when speaking [S6].

**Willingness to rework.** Don't be afraid to redraw in search of the best solution to tell the story, and if part of a drawing doesn't work, cut it out and rework it [S2]. Glebas also passes on his mentor Vance Gerry's rule: "If you can't photocopy it, trace it. If you can't trace it, then you'll have to draw it" [S7].

**Expressiveness.** Draw bold and expressive; show how a character feels by feeling the pose and the emotion in your own body as you draw [S5]. A person is always "doing" something, so express the purpose and experience the pose kinetically in your own body [S5].

**Design and line quality.** Avoid symmetry — it's boring and makes drawings look cut out — and instead use angles to avoid symmetry and rigid poses, since dynamic asymmetry is much more exciting [S5]. Play straight lines against curves for interest [S2], use straight line symbols for stretches and bent line symbols for squashes [S5], and darken pupils when drawing eyes [S2].

**Composition and anatomy.** Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S5], and watch the body's landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S5]. The book's clarity chapter adds the related rule that you should be able to black in a drawing and still read what's happening, keeping decoration inside the main outline so drawings don't get busy, and making those outlines interesting [S1].

The context throughout is cinematic rather than fine-art: the book is about directing the story through storyboards, so these tips target the people who visualize film shots — directors, storyboard artists, and animators. The constant framing in terms of telling the story, choosing camera angles, and composing to a drawn border makes that purpose explicit, and Vance Gerry, the origin of the photocopy/trace advice, is identified as a storyboard artist and mentor in that tradition [S7].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The book treats these as two approaches to the same job — converting color image data optimized for one display into data optimized for another — where the choice is driven entirely by how different the two displays and their viewing environments are [S2].

| | **Transcoding** | **Color rerendering** |
|---|---|---|
| **When used** | Displays match in black level, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma; only the primary chromaticities differ [S2] | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S1] |
| **Procedure** | Linearize the first display's encoded RGB → convert to CIE XYZ → convert to the second display's RGB values → re-impose the encoding nonlinearity [S2] | Undo whatever color rendering was implicitly or explicitly done for the first display, then color render the CIE XYZ values for the second display [S1] |
| **Essentially** | A purely numeric chromaticity conversion between otherwise matched displays | A re-rendering of the image's appearance for a new viewing environment |

So transcoding only works when the rendering intent is already a match and just the colorimetric coordinates differ; rerendering becomes necessary when the appearance itself — contrast, white level, surround — would otherwise carry over incorrectly, and the solution is to strip the first rendering back to scene values and render them anew [S1][S2].

In the cinema context, the book defines color rendering in the color-science sense as the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment — its example is a JPEG captured and rendered for desert sunlight being viewed on an office monitor with peak white far dimmer than the sun [S4]. That's why scene-referred camera raw needs color rendering done downstream before the shot is shown in a theater, and why rendering baked in by the camera in a non-raw format is harder to undo than to perform [S6]. The ACES workflow institutionalizes this split: the RRT applies color appearance rendering for dark-surround theatrical viewing, the ODT then adapts that rendered data to each display device, and the RRT deliberately collects the transforms common to all ODTs — including picture rendering to the viewing environment — so they don't get repeated per device [S3][S9][S13].

results.question: What does the book say about FACE OFF?
results.answer:
The retrieved corpus contains no discussion of the film *Face/Off* (John Woo, 1997), so there is no book analysis of it to report — that specific topic is simply absent from the evidence.

The closest material concerns facial techniques, not the movie. The VES Handbook describes **"Face Paste"**, the classic facial motion-capture method in which an actor's face is captured separately in a high-resolution camera volume and pasted onto body animation [S9]. A cinematic-storytelling source covers **face reveals** — scenes where a hidden face is shown by lowering binoculars, removing a mask or hood, stepping into a streetlamp, or opening curtains [S10]. And several FACS sources detail how facial movements are scored and coded [S1][S11–S13]. None of these analyzes *Face/Off*.

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The handbook’s central claim is that affect, fatigue, and injury are control states — internal conditions that must change later action selection and execution, not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen [S3]. They belong to the layered representation’s dimensional layer, which guides the selection and timing of lower-level controls without dictating one fixed pose [S1]. The cinematic payoff is continuity: a committed state persists and constrains everything after it, so in the specimen fight IR Mara’s right-shoulder injury “begins at state.v2 and persists through the final frame,” and every clip must begin from the previous clip’s accepted terminal state [S14].

**The three states as mechanisms**

| State | How it’s represented | What it changes downstream |
|---|---|---|
| Affect | Dimensional valence / arousal / dominance, updated by appraisal [S1][S3] | Attention, recovery urgency and cleanliness, risk tolerance [S3] |
| Fatigue | Compiler-state recurrence; global exertion plus local limb capacity [S4][S5] | Step-width variability, stabilization time, trunk compensation [S5] |
| Injury | Object with capacity multipliers, compensations, stated uncertainty [S6] | Load distribution between legs, stance timing, trunk lean in recovery [S6] |

**Affect** is a continuous trajectory in valence, arousal, and dominance, useful for interpolation and temporal arcs [S1]. It is explicitly underdetermined: the same high-arousal negative state could read as fear, anger, pain, or disgust depending on appraisal, context, and action tendencies [S1]. The handbook implements it as an appraisal update — a trigger (an expected interception fails, a lane opens) yields goal congruence, controllability, and certainty scores that move priors to posteriors, with concrete behavioral effects: attention narrows toward the exit lane, recovery becomes urgent but mechanically less clean, and risk tolerance rises for one recovery attempt [S3].

**Fatigue** is defined as a compiler state, not remaining capacity: `f = clamp(f + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1)`, with the warning that those terms must be calibrated, not inferred from prose [S4]. It splits into global exertion (RPE 6.5, breath cycle 1.25 s, recovery rate per second) and local per-limb capacity (left leg 0.46, right leg 0.78, right shoulder 0.63), producing coordination effects like increased step-width variability and longer stabilization after hard redirection [S5]. Balance over time — exertion versus recuperation — is what prevents injury, fatigue, boredom, and burnout, and the same logic shows up in machine design, e.g., Apple’s breathing-style indicator light for on/off/sleep/charging states [S2].

**Injury** is specified as a state object: region, pain, severity, and mechanical effects (load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off capacity) plus compensations — favoring the right leg, shortening the left stance interval, increasing trunk lean during emergency recovery — with an explicit uncertainty field noting the source is dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement, at 0.70 confidence [S6].

**How control reads on screen**

The supporting material shows how these states surface as visible control. Laban-style effort states pair two effort factors into six states — mobile (flow+time), stable (weight+space), remote (flow+space), rhythm (weight+time), dream (weight+flow), awake (space+time) — each with four configurations, such as mobile’s startled freeze, taffy pulling, popping popcorn, and sighing in relief [S7][S8][S9]. Control itself is conveyed by symmetry: a natural, symmetrical posture reads as deliberate agency, while a contorted, mismatched shape reads as pain, leverage, or involuntary reaction — the more you contort, the more the audience assumes you are doing it because you have to [S13]. Pain also leaks through breath and voice: injuries near the body’s center tend to lower vocal pitch, peripheral injuries tend to raise it, and adrenaline can blunt immediate awareness of injury [S11]. Weariness is drawn through the pushed-out chin, curved back, forward body, sweat, frayed hair, and dirt — while keeping the character “tired but hasn’t lost his fighting spirit” [S12].

One aspect the corpus leaves incomplete: injury is asserted as a control state and its object is fully specified, but no formal mechanism shows how injury feeds back into action selection the way the affect appraisal update and the fatigue recurrence do — the other sources treat injury as something expressed (posture, voice, breath) rather than as a state that drives later choices. A temperament source adds that fully absorbed performers can be oblivious to pain and fatigue in the heat of action, which illustrates appraisal-based gating but is not a cinema framework [S10]. A natural next step would be drafting that missing injury-update rule in the same shape as `affect_update`.

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
In cinema, an object's movement is never read on its own — it's read against the background, which acts as the stationary reference frame that makes motion visible. Bruce Block's *The Visual Story* gives the core definition: movement exists only when an object changes position in relation to the frame line or a second, stationary object; no positional change means no movement, and the strongest possible contrast to movement is no movement at all, as in tableau staging [S3][S4][S13]. Every moving object generates a track (its path), and tracks are categorized four ways: direction, quality, scale, and speed [S6].

The sources describe several distinct mechanisms for how object and background interact:

- **Induced movement:** a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary one appears to move instead. Block's forest example: the car drives in a circle, the camera pans to keep it framed, and the trees sweep the opposite way — the viewer assigns that background motion to the car even though the car never moves within the frame [S2][S14].
- **Motion parallax:** Mascelli's *Five C's* describes moving players and camera so that objects cover and uncover one another, producing a variation in image travel for objects at different distances from the lens — this conveys position and distance in the setting and is what makes object-to-background movement readable in depth [S10].
- **Tracking alongside:** Brown considers tracking the simplest, most clearly motivated camera move — a parallel track beside a character or vehicle emphasizes the moving background and the sweep of the motion [S15].
- **Lens-perspective tricks:** with a telephoto lens on a circular tracking move, the background appears to revolve quickly behind a static subject; that apparent speed increases with the subject's distance, the camera's circling speed, and the focal length, which makes it a tool for visualizing a character's psychological breakdown [S9].
- **Match moving in post:** when the foreground camera moves, the background must move correspondingly — tracking data extracted from the foreground footage is applied to the background during compositing, a process called match moving [S7], the same workflow DaVinci Resolve's tracker automates when attaching elements to footage [S5].

The one warning case is motion blur: a blurred object over a neutral background is fairly easy to extract, but over a detailed background the soft matte inevitably pulls background detail into the cutout [S1]. The through-line across all these techniques is that the background is the reference the audience trusts — filmmakers stage, lens, or composite the background's motion to control what the object's movement means.

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
All five books agree on the core idea: **sound editing is the postproduction phase where the soundtrack is built and mixed, and its job is to make the visuals work.** It is where the sound the production didn't capture gets created, and it demands far more decisions than the picture edit because a single wrong choice can undermine the visuals [S1].

## What sound editing is

Sound design is described as "an aural universe" made of layered dialogue, sound effects, music, ambient atmospheres, and sometimes voice-over [S7]. The sound designer's creative input is likened to the director of photography's for picture: they own the overall acoustic experience and oversee the individual dialogue, ambience, hard-effect, and foley tracks [S6]. How the edit proceeds depends on genre, content, purpose, the quality of the sound assets, and how it will be presented — yet careful building and mixing of tracks is required at every scale, from a two-track music video to a 62-track blockbuster [S4].

## How the sound edit proceeds

The process follows the picture edit in stages:

1. During the rough cut, only the tracks needed for dramatic decisions are edited — typically dialogue with occasional scratch music [S7].
2. After picture lock, the editor and sound designer build the multi-track sound design one track at a time, usually 6–16 tracks for a simple film [S7].
3. Tracks are equalized and mixed down to a master — stereo at minimum, 5.1 surround for cinema [S7]. Feature-film mixes can reach up to 60 tracks [S13].

Within that workflow, the editor gathers additional audio in post to augment or replace production sound, sometimes generating a "more-realistic-sounding reality" than what was recorded [S9]. Specific techniques include separating effects so the mixer can fade one out and another in smoothly, or running a continuous sound across two disparate visuals to imply a link between scenes; the mix can separate or link, and can imply either the passage or the continuity of time [S13]. During sound editing the editor can also manipulate speed and pitch of material [S2]. The sound editor is expected to create the overall design and transmit it to the director and the re-recording mixer [S3]. Tools matter here too: DaVinci Resolve's Fairlight page is built into the edit suite so sound, picture, VFX, and color can all be refined up to mastering, including recording voice-over and cleaning background hum [S10].

## Priorities and principles

Two goals dominate. **Believability** is called the most urgent task of the sound edit: sound is processed more rapidly than visuals, so if it doesn't seem believable the visuals are undermined and audience involvement is lost [S11]. **Narrative clarity** is the other: the editor's first task is determining the narrative point of the scene, and that point must be supported or "surrounded" by sound — as with the authenticity that is central to *The Battle of Algiers* [S1][S11]. The underlying reason creative sound matters so much is that auditory stimuli affect humans on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels; even "silent" films were never intended to be silent, only technologically limited [S5].

Two notes on what the sources do and don't cover: the collected books say sound effects fall into four main categories, but the retrieved excerpt cuts off before naming them [S8]. And historically, early sound technology so restricted editing — discs and Movietone couldn't be cut without losing sync — that editing was limited to silent sequences until re-recording and multiple-camera shooting became common [S14].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The advice "write radio sparely" comes from *Hey Whipple Squeeze This*, and it's the book's most repeated commandment for radio: cut the copy to the bone so the delivery has room to breathe and the silence does the selling.

The reasoning runs through several chapters. Unless a concept genuinely demands a flood of fast words, spare writing lets voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2]. Overwriting is called the most common mistake people make in radio, and the prescribed remedy is blunt: "Be a genius. Underwrite" [S3]. Time pressure points the same way — if a :60 is a house, a :30 is a tent, and clients' promotional tags cut into the remaining seconds, you have to write sparely from the start [S1].

The one concrete technique the book offers is to **write the mandatories first**: draft the required legal copy (its example is the fine print at the end of a bank spot) as sparely as possible, time it, and treat what's left over as the space your commercial has to fit [S3]. Then trust silence, which the book calls radio's answer to white space in print: "silence enlarges the idea it surrounds" [S8]. Because radio's canvas can stretch to impossible things — an armored division crashing through a mall to buy burgers — a spare script isn't a constraint; it leaves room for the listener's imagination to fill the picture [S13].

Two adjacent notes from other sources in the corpus reinforce the approach: radio needs frequency to work, so even a great spot must be repeated often [S9], and because listeners tire quickly of a single commercial, the near-zero production cost of radio is best used to make several spots [S15].
